Title: Stem cells: From hope to cure - avoiding the hype
NewsSummary: In his keynote address in the APAN annual meeting, Professor El Nasir Lalani calls for regulation of stem cell research to discourage its unproven clinical application

content.text: Professor El Nasir Lalani was invited as a keynote speaker at the 51st annual meeting of the Asia Pacific Advanced Network (APAN), held virtually on February 3, 2021. His presentation covered: non-communicable diseases (NCDs) and their impact on morbidity, mortality with particular reference to the low-to-middle-income countries (LMICs); potential applications of stem cells and regenerative medicine to cure NCDs; and the need for building local/regional capacity in basic sciences and translational medicine.
Here are some takeaways from the keynote speech:

The application of stem cell research to treat NCDs such as Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, cancer, diabetes, ischemic heart disease, hold significant promise. Over 80% of premature NCD related deaths occur in LMICs. The economic implications of these diseases are daunting for these countries. Regenerative medicine applications of stem cells to NCDs are starting to be trialled and offer hope for affordable cure which could positively impact health care and economies of LMICs.

Professor Lalani drew attention to the dire need for building local and regional research capacity if LMICs such as Pakistan wish to make the therapeutic benefits of stem cells accessible to their people. He proposed a partnership model among stem cell research institutions, industry and individuals across the Asia Pacific region and other parts of the world to galvanise capacity building by attracting the brightest minds and stopping brain drain. Professor Lalani reflected on the potential role of APAN in creating partnerships, connecting people, and nurturing and sharing knowledge and expertise. Such a model could help local researchers enhance their capacity by collaborating with experienced scientists and researchers internationally. As an example, he shared the AKU-CRM model that allows early-career researchers, inducted at the Centre, to work in close partnership with experts at the University of California, San Francisco, on various research programmes.

Highlighting the potential application of stem cell research, Professor Lalani cautioned against the worldwide trend of clinics offering unproven, potentially dangerous stem cell treatments that cost thousands of dollars to patients. Such clinics use social media, websites, questionable research publications and word of mouth to create a hype and lure patients into availing these treatments. Instead of curing diseases, these unproven treatments are causing health issues such as the growth of tumours and cancer in patients. Professor Lalani emphasised the need for educating people about unproven treatments and called for legislation to regulate stem cell research and discourage its unproven clinical application. Otherwise, it could result in more health damage than benefit with adverse implications for the stem cell research itself.

Responding to questions from the audience, Professor Lalani underscored that there are ethical concerns associated with stem cell research and its application that require candid discussions. Setting the ethical boundaries for stem cell research requires a lot more thinking and public engagement which a network like APAN could facilitate. However, he also reminded us that every country's response to the ethical issues would vary depending upon their religious, cultural and social worldview and affiliations.
